blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and with a many-step sampler these rollouts typically dominate the cost of training. Few-step models cut this cost, yet they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives are built for an instantaneous velocity with a many-step sampler. We adapt RL objectives to few-step models systematically in three phases, namely a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation to $x$-space expresses each objective we consider through a common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly marked level for transition or flow-map objectives, so that objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become comparable. The decomposition writes the gradient of each of these objectives as the sum of a self-regression toward a reference and a reward augmentation, so that a method reduces, at the gradient level, to a choice of anchors and weights. The adaptation computes each anchor from a few-step model at the end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself or from an auxiliary network. This yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL in one modular codebase. In our experiments, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective when the reward is differentiable and its gradient is affordable; otherwise DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few iterations despite a sometimes higher per-iteration cost. Extra inference steps show no systematic aggregate benefit in our experiments, although selected outputs visibly improve with two to four times as many sampling steps as in training.
blocks.zh: 加强学习(RL)已经成为推广模式的标准培训后方法,但大多数RL目标在每个周期都推出现行政策,而且随着一个多步骤的取样器,这些推广通常主导培训成本。 很少步骤模型削减了这一成本,然而它们在一个间隔时间中模拟平均速度,而现有的RL目标则是用一个多步骤取样器为瞬时速度构建的。 我们分三个阶段,即转变、分解和适应阶段,系统地使生殖健康目标适应几个步骤的模式。 向美元-空间的转变体现了我们通过共同的政策预测所考虑的每个目标,即默认的清洁终点和明确标明的过渡或流动图目标水平,从而使所表述的密度、速度或回报等目标具有可比性。 分解法将每个这些目标的梯度写成自回归到参照和奖励增益的总和,这样一种方法在梯度上会降低到选择锚和权重的程度. 适应用从网络本身或从辅助网络中恢复的瞬时速度计算出每个锚在运输末端或正切线沿线的几步模型。 这在一个模块化的代码库中产生了FlowGRPO,AWM,DifmusionNFT,DifmusionOPSD和ReFL的几步版本. 在我们的实验中,以奖励为基础的方法在奖励是不同的而且其梯度可以承受的情况下最为有效;否则,分散式NFT式的方法一般在相对较少的重复中获得很高的奖励,尽管有时每次渗透的成本较高。 额外的推断步骤表明,我们的实验没有系统的总体效益,尽管选定的产出明显改进,抽样步骤是培训的2至4倍。

blocks.en:
Diffusion models and their flow-matching counterparts generate data by
integrating a learned transport from noise to samples, and have become a
dominant approach to image and video synthesis ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) .
Because the learned field is accurate only locally, sampling typically takes tens of
network evaluations ( Song et al., 2021a ) .

blocks.en:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for
diffusion models. Fine-tuning against reward models of human preference, text rendering or
composition measurably improves the outputs ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Xue et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ) .
This gain, however, typically requires samples from the current policy at every
iteration and must be protected against reward hacking, in which the policy
exploits the reward model instead of improving.

time and memory of training, and more so for long video sequences. A few-step

blocks.en:
This paper builds one in three phases ( Figure 2 ), namely a
transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation maps each
objective to x x -space. Under a linear noise schedule, a velocity defines an affine map
between noise levels, so each objective we consider can be expressed through a
common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly
marked level for transition or flow-map objectives. In x x -space, objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become
directly comparable. The decomposition splits the loss gradient.
The gradient of every objective we consider is the sum of a self-regression
term, which keeps the policy close to a reference, and a reward-augmentation
term, which contains the reward, so that, at the gradient level, a method reduces to a choice of
anchors and weights. The adaptation extends the anchors to few-step models. We
show
how each anchor is computed from a few-step model, either at the end of its
transport or along the tangent of the trajectory, with the instantaneous
velocity recovered from the network itself, as in MeanFlow, or from an
auxiliary network, as in DMD.

blocks.en:
All methods share one codebase, which is represented by a single training step
with several method-specific stages, namely rollout, reward and advantage, anchors
and weights, and loss (plus auxiliary fitting and the refresh of the old
policy), where each method overrides only the hooks in which it differs
(§ 5 ). The methods are therefore compared under shared rollout,
reward and evaluation code, and a new variant is specified mainly by its
anchors and weights.
Experimentally, we compare seven implementations on image generation with an
AnyFlow-distilled SD3.5-Medium ( Stability AI, 2024 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , under
a non-differentiable OCR reward and a differentiable mixed reward, and on video
generation with an AnyFlow-distilled Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B ( Team Wan et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) ; we further test whether the fine-tuned
few-step models improve when sampled with more steps.

blocks.en:
The contributions of this paper are as follows. • A general view. After the transformation to x x -space, the gradients of the RL objectives considered here share one
decoupled form, the sum of a self-regression term and a reward-augmentation
term, so that their gradients differ only in their anchors and weights. • A systematic adaptation to few-step models. Each of these anchors can be
computed from an average-velocity model at the end of the transport or along its
tangent, which yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT,
DiffusionOPSD and ReFL within one modular codebase. • Empirical guidance with experimental analysis. Where the reward is differentiable and its
gradient affordable, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective in our experiments, and ReFL
alone is a strong baseline. Otherwise, group-advantage methods apply. Among
them, DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few
iterations, even when one iteration is expensive, and DMD-based variants are
faster per iteration on image but slower on video, depending on the relative
cost of forward and backward passes, and often coincide with larger
held-out degradation. Additional inference steps bring little aggregate
improvement in generation quality, while visual gains appear in selected outputs with
more sampling steps than training.

blocks.en: 2 Background
blocks.zh: 2 背景情况

blocks.en:
Diffusion models learn to reverse a fixed noising process ( Ho et al., 2020 ) ; score-based models cast this reversal as a reverse-time
SDE whose probability-flow ODE gives a deterministic sampler, of which DDIM is
a discrete instance ( Song et al., 2021b ; Song et al., 2021a ) . Flow matching and
rectified flow instead regress the velocity of a prescribed interpolation
between noise and data, the latter straightening the paths so that fewer
integration steps suffice ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) .
These models were scaled by moving to a latent space ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , by
transformer backbones ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Ma et al., 2024 ) and by larger, more
efficient architectures ( Podell et al., 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2025a ) ,
with classifier-free guidance as a standard way to trade diversity for
prompt fidelity ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . Related generators include
current text-to-image systems ( OpenAI, 2022 ; Betker et al., 2023 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2025 ; Team Seedream et al., 2025 ; Z-Image Team et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2025 ) ,
multimodal models that both generate and understand images in one network ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Ma et al., 2025a ; Xie et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2024b ; OpenAI et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025a ) ,
trained on web-scale image–text data ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ; Zou, 2024 ) , and video
generators such as Wan and LongCat-Video ( Team Wan et al., 2025 ; Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2025 ) . These models typically learn the
instantaneous velocity of the sampling flow, or an affine transformation of it
such as the score or the predicted noise. Since this velocity is instantaneous,
the sampler integrates it with many small steps, typically 32 or 64, which
makes inference costly.

blocks.en:
Sampling cost has been cut along several lines. Progressive distillation halves
the number of steps repeatedly by training a student to match two teacher
steps with one ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) . Consistency models map every
point of a trajectory to its endpoint, and were extended to latent space,
arbitrary trajectory jumps, multiple sub-intervals and segmented trajectories ( Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023a ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ; Ren et al., 2024 ) ;
consistency has also been used as a training regulariser against sampling
drift and to learn from noisy data ( Daras et al., 2023 ; Daras et al., 2024 ) . Shortcut
models condition on the step size and learn to take large steps directly ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . Adversarial distillation adds a discriminator so
that one to four steps produce sharp samples ( Wang et al., 2023a ; Sauer et al., 2025 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Chadebec et al., 2025 ; Lu and Song, 2025 ) .
Distribution matching distillation (DMD) trains the generator so that its
output distribution matches the teacher’s, using the difference between a
teacher score and the score of an auxiliary network fitted to the generator’s
samples ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ) , an idea shared with Diff-Instruct and
variational score distillation ( Luo et al., 2023b ; Wang et al., 2023b ) ;
later work scales it to flow models, splits it into
sub-intervals, decouples guidance from matching, moves it to continuous time,
regularises it with consistency, and adapts it to video ( Ge et al., 2026a ; Fan et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Ge et al., 2026b ; Nie et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) .
Flow maps learn the transport between any two noise levels. MeanFlow
parameterises the average velocity over an interval and trains it through its
identity with the instantaneous velocity ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Geng et al., 2026 ) , and AnyFlow distils such a
map on policy for any step count ( Gu et al., 2026 ) . Unlike the many-step
generators above, these flow-map models learn an average velocity over an
interval, which can be read as the direction of a secant of the sampling
trajectory, differing substantially from the instantaneous velocity where the
trajectory is curved.

blocks.en:
RL fine-tuning of generators builds on policy optimisation ( Levine, 2018 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) , preference optimisation ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) and group-relative advantages, which normalise rewards
within a group of samples for the same prompt ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . For diffusion models, early
work fine-tunes on human feedback ( Lee et al., 2023 ) , treats denoising as
a Markov decision process optimised by policy gradients ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ) , or optimises pairwise preferences directly ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) . FlowGRPO brings group-relative policy
optimisation to flow models by turning the ODE sampler into an SDE with
tractable transition likelihoods ( Liu et al., 2025a ) ; follow-ups extend it
to video, mix ODE and SDE steps, weight timesteps, and preserve the noise
coefficients of the sampler ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ; He et al., 2026 ; Wang and Yu, 2025 ) . A
second family avoids transition likelihoods by acting on the forward process:
AWM weights the pretraining loss by the advantage ( Xue et al., 2026 ) ,
reward-weighted and policy-gradient flow matching reweight or rescale the
velocity regression ( Fan et al., 2025 ; McAllister et al., 2026 ) ,
adjoint matching is scaled to RL post-training ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) , and
DiffusionNFT contrasts positive and negative implicit policies built from the
model and the frozen policy that generated its rollouts ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) , following NFT in
language models ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . A third family backpropagates
differentiable rewards through the sampler, as in DRaFT and ReFL ( Clark et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) ; the recently
proposed DiffusionOPSD ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) belongs to this family
but constructs detached points with normalised reward-gradient steps and fits
the policy to them, thereby forming a surrogate gradient. These methods are
built for an instantaneous velocity, and most of them need on-policy
rollouts at every iteration, which are expensive with the many-step samplers discussed above; how
to apply RL to few-step models is therefore an important question.

blocks.en:
Closest to this paper are methods that fine-tune few-step models with rewards.
Several combine DMD with RL, by adding a reward term to distillation, guiding
distillation with reward gradients, or recasting distribution matching itself
as a reward ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026a ) ;
others tune distilled models with non-differentiable rewards,
Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularised
alignment or pairwise sample optimisation ( Luo et al., 2026 ; Luo, 2025 ; Miao et al., 2025 ) . For flow maps,
Flow-Map GRPO composes stochastic steps of a flow-map generator ( Li et al., 2026b ) , MeanFlowNFT applies DiffusionNFT to an
average-velocity model through its self-induced instantaneous field ( Huang et al., 2026b ) , and RTDMD optimises a reward-tilted distribution
matching objective ( Huang et al., 2026a ) . These works mostly adapt one objective
to one kind of few-step model; we instead give a common construction that
extends FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL to
average-velocity models, and compare them under one implementation.

blocks.en:
Each RL method of § 3.2 increases the relative probability of
high-reward samples under the rollout distribution p old p_{\mathrm{old}} of the
old policy. The methods
differ in the space in which the update is formulated (transition densities,
velocities, or rewards differentiated through the sample) and in how a
few-step network computes the quantities that the update requires. This
section resolves both differences in three steps, summarised in Figure 2 . (i) Transformation to x x -space (§ 4.1 , Figure 2 a). Under the linear noise schedule a velocity transports a state
affinely, so each objective of § 3 can be expressed through a
common prediction in x x -space. By default this prediction is the policy
prediction x ~ θ \tilde{x}_{\theta} ; MeanFlow and FewStepGRPO keep an explicitly marked level- r r quantity.
In x x -space the methods become directly comparable. (ii) Decomposition of the gradient (§ 4.2 , Figure 2 b). In x x -space, the gradient of each of these losses is the transposed Jacobian ( ∂ x ~ θ / ∂ θ ) ⊤ (\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta)^{\top} applied to the sum of a reward-free
self-regression toward an anchor x ~ reg \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}} , which limits how far the prediction
moves, and a reward augmentation along x ~ rwd − x ~ base \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}} , which contains the
reward. A method is then specified by the prediction, three anchors ( x ~ reg , x ~ rwd , x ~ base ) (\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}},\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}},\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}) and three weights ( W reg , W rwd , ω ) (W_{\mathrm{reg}},W_{\mathrm{rwd}},\omega) instead of a new loss. (iii) Adaptation to few-step models (§ 4.3 , Figure 2 c). The framework requires instantaneous velocities,
whereas a few-step model outputs an average velocity. Its anchors are
therefore computed either at the end of the transport curve (u-form) or along
the tangent at the current state (v-form). The latter recovers the
instantaneous velocity from the network itself, as in MeanFlow, or from an
auxiliary network, as in DMD. § 5 then specifies the predictions, anchors and weights of each
family.

differentiable reward through a single late denoising step. Classic ReFL stops
a rollout of the old-policy sampler at a small noise level t t without gradient and

evaluation; as in Example 8 , we instead evaluate the network at the

blocks.en:
The framework of § 4 is implemented as one base trainer whose
method step runs one outer iteration. Each trainer of
§§ 5.3 – 5.6 is a subclass that overrides
a few stage methods, and the instantaneous-velocity estimator of § 4.3 , v-ind or v-aux , is a separate object passed to the trainer.
Here v-ind uses the
MeanFlow identity with the shared old-policy correction J J to construct an
instantaneous velocity from an average velocity, whereas v-aux uses an auxiliary velocity to
approximate the instantaneous velocity of the old-policy rollout distribution p old p_{\mathrm{old}} (which DMD takes to be p θ p_{\theta} ), as in Equation ( 52 ). Stages 1 and 2 below operate on groups, since they
produce and score the K K members of a prompt, and keep the index ( i ) (i) as in
§§ 3 – 4.3 . From Stage 3 onward the framework acts
on one member at a time. The prediction, the
three anchors and the three weights are per-sample quantities; the index ( i ) (i) is omitted in the equations and in the loss terms ℒ reg \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}} , ℒ rwd \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}} , and becomes the leading batch axis in code.

iteration rolls out with it.

The trainers differ mainly in this stage. It receives the detached rollout and
returns the current prediction, the anchors and the detached coefficients;
FewStepOPSD returns branch-indexed tuples for its rewarded anchors and ω \omega .
We describe it in four parts, namely (i) the query levels, (ii) the two ways to
compute the clean prediction, (iii) the two estimators of the instantaneous
velocity that these predictions require, and (iv) the weights.

blocks.en:
FewStepAWM adapts Equation ( 17 ) as one clipped reward-augmentation term
on the matching residual of the model. It has no explicit self-regression term,
and in MeanFlowAWM the reward displacement is measured from the detached current prediction.

而在MeanFlowAWM中,悬赏流离是从离散的当前预测中衡量出来的。

blocks.en:
Stage 1 uses the deterministic rollout, n it = n ts n_{\mathrm{it}}=n_{\mathrm{ts}} ,
and every inner iteration draws a fresh ( t , r , ϵ ) (t,r,\epsilon) , re-noises the

blocks.en: 5.6 FewStepOPSD: Extended Reward Augmentation and ReFL
blocks.zh: 5.6 少数步骤OPSD:扩展奖励增强和ReFL

blocks.en:
FewStepOPSD belongs to the family of reward-gradient-based methods ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) and is related
to gradient-guided distribution matching ( Dong et al., 2026 ) .
It implements Example 8 (iii) as a FewStepNFT trainer whose rewarded
points are constructed from the reward gradient instead of sampled; it
therefore uses the normalisers of Equation ( 105 ), and its configuration
with a single ascent step is the ReFL proxy of Example 9 . It modifies
more stages than FewStepNFT. Stage 1 depends on the reward, the rewarded
anchors are constructed points instead of rollout samples, and Stage 4
overrides loss . Stage 2 is unchanged, and r ^ \hat{r} enters
only through the weights.
blocks.zh:
少斯捷普OPSD属于以奖励为基础的方法家族(徐等,2023;克拉克等,2024;王等,2026)并有关联.
改为梯度制导分布比对(Dong等人,2026年) .
它执行例8(三),作为 " 少先队NFT " 的培训员,其奖励
积分由奖励梯度而不是抽样构建;
因此,使用方程式的常态(105)及其配置
单升阶是例9的 ReFL 代理。 它改变了
比"少时节"(NEWSTEPNFT)还多. 第一阶段取决于奖励,奖励
锚是构造的点,而不是推出样品,以及第四阶段
覆盖损失 。 第2阶段不变, R ^\ hat{r} 输入
只有通过重量。

blocks.en:
FewStepOPSD uses the reward-coupled rollout Equation ( 82 ). It first draws the i.i.d. base samples with Equation ( 81 ). The reward-coupled construction then applies Equation ( 62 ), taking M tgt M_{\mathrm{tgt}} normalised reward-gradient steps in
each direction from the r = 0 r=0 prediction x ~ old , u \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} , with the displacement
transferred to the anchor by Equation ( 70 ), giving x ~ ± \tilde{x}_{\pm} .
The points x ~ ± \tilde{x}_{\pm} are detached, so the computation graph of the reward
ends here and the policy update does not back-propagate through the decoder or
the reward model; the reward must be differentiable.

在此结束, 策略更新不会通过解码器反向推进或
奖励模式;奖励必须不同。

above, with the changes below. Stage 1 takes a single ascent step, M tgt = 1 M_{\mathrm{tgt}}=1 , without a

and its displacement is added back by Equation ( 70 ), so ∇ R \nabla R is
evaluated at x ~ old , u \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} as specified by Equation ( 78 ).
Stage 2 is not used, because ReFL has no advantage; ω 1 > 0 \omega_{1}>0 is fixed by

The ReFL override keeps the factor c adv c_{\mathrm{adv}} of Equation ( 107 ). Stage 3 keeps the same
anchors. Stage 4 keeps only ℒ rwd , 1 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd},1} with W reg = 0 W_{\mathrm{reg}}=0 , i.e. the loss of Section 5.6 reduces to its
ascent term ( Section 5.6 ). The resulting gradient is that of Equation ( 79 ), the few-step form of Equation ( 77 ).

blocks.en: 6 Experiment
blocks.zh: 6 实验

blocks.en:
Having established a general view of these methods, we use experiments to
answer three questions. Every trainer of
§§ 5.3 – 5.6 implements one of these
methods, minimises the same loss form, and differs mainly in its anchors and
weights. (i) Which of these choices, in particular the reward signal and the
estimator of the instantaneous velocity, determine how effectively and how
efficiently a few-step generator is fine-tuned, and how strongly it exploits the
reward? (ii) Do these
conclusions carry over to a different modality, or do they show limitations in
other scenarios? (iii) Does a generator fine-tuned at a few steps improve when
it is sampled with more steps, without retraining?

奖励? (二) 这样做
结论转而采用另一种方式,或者它们是否在以下方面表现出局限性:
其他情况? (三) 发电机的微调在几步内是否有所改善,何时
它的样本有 更多的步骤, 不再培训?

Each outer iteration draws two batches, each with 2 2 prompts per rank and K = 16 K=16 members, on 32 32 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, i.e. 2048 2048 rollouts per outer iteration. We use AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) with
learning rate 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} and gradient-norm clipping at 1 1 ; u old u_{\mathrm{old}} is an
EMA of u θ u_{\theta} refreshed once per outer iteration; for the NFT/OPSD families, β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 and c adv = 5 c_{\mathrm{adv}}=5 in Equation ( 84 ); the KL-u penalty
against the fixed AnyFlow initial policy uses Equation ( 92 ) with weight 10 − 4 10^{-4} ; and each member is
queried n ts = 4 n_{\mathrm{ts}}=4 times, with half of each batch set to r = t r=t and a
quarter to r = 0 r=0 .
For FewStepOPSD and ReFL, the world size is 48 48 instead, because
computing the gradient with respect to the video latents requires much memory,
while the per-rank batch is unchanged. FewStepOPSD and ReFL therefore use 3072 3072 rollouts per outer iteration, 1.5 1.5 times as many as the 32-GPU runs.
The runs are thus matched in the number of outer iterations but not in the
number of samples, and the quality comparison should be interpreted with this
caveat. GPU-hours remain comparable across runs, whereas s/iter is reported but
is not comparable across runs with different world sizes.

blocks.en:
Using the same four reward components as the
LongCat/MeanFlowNFT video setup ( Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026b ) , we define our training
reward as an unweighted sum. The HPSv3 scorer ( Ma et al., 2025b ) enters through
HPSv3-general and HPSv3-percentile (per-frame, the latter the mean of the top 30 % 30\% of frames under the caption); VideoAlign’s motion quality (MQ) and text
alignment (TA) are drawn from video-feedback scoring ( Liu et al., 2025b ) . MQ and TA are z z -normalised before
entering the sum; tables report their raw scorer outputs.
Only HPSv3 is differentiable here, and its two reductions account for 96 % 96\% of the aggregate reward under the z z -normalised weights
( Section D.5 ). The VideoAlign reward takes file paths as
input and decodes the videos in its own pipeline, so there is no differentiable
path from the latents to this reward. FewStepOPSD and ReFL therefore use only
the gradients of the HPSv3 terms, while they are evaluated on all four
terms; Section D.5 quantifies this asymmetry, which does not
occur in the image setting.

blocks.en:
Table 6 and Figures 4 and 4 support
the following observations. (i) The adaptation of § 4.3 is beneficial in these runs, and the
v-prediction form gives better performance in most of these comparisons
( Figures 6 and 1 ). FewStepGRPO raises the
training reward from 1.450 1.450 to 1.461 1.461 and the held-out HPSv3 from 10.30 10.30 to 11.58 11.58 , whereas FlowGRPO, its counterpart with direct employment of average-velocity, leaves the
training reward at 1.438 1.438 and lowers HPSv3 to 9.62 9.62 . Meanwhile, MeanFlowNFT as
the v-prediction counterpart of DiffusionNFT, which is the direct employment of
average-velocity, reaches a training
reward of 1.509 1.509 against 1.440 1.440 , and is higher on the
held-out HPSv3 ( 13.23 13.23 against 11.79 11.79 ), ImageReward ( 1.385 1.385 against 1.317 1.317 ) and best GenEval2 ( 0.411 0.411 against 0.399 0.399 ), the last within the ∼ 0.03 {\sim}0.03 resolution. (ii) In the OCR setting, DMDAWM, MeanFlowNFT and DMDNFT raise OCR accuracy
from 0.498 0.498 to at least 0.85 0.85 within 100 100 – 150 150 iterations, whereas
MeanFlowAWM and FewStepGRPO reach only 0.802 0.802 and 0.776 0.776 at iteration 200 200 .
Furthermore, it can be observed that within the 200 200 -iteration horizon of Figure 4 , the highest logged OCR
accuracy is reached by MeanFlowNFT, about 0.945 0.945 at iteration 150 150 , and it
is also the first to reach 0.85 0.85 , at iteration 100 100 . DMDAWM starts lower at
iteration 50 50 but rises steeply thereafter and
reaches 0.936 0.936 at iteration 200 200 , where the two curves coincide within the
resolution of the plot ( Table 6 a). Its rapid rise is consistent with a combination of two properties. (i) It has no self-regression
( x ~ reg = ∅ \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing ), so only reward augmentation contributes to its
decoupled update. (ii) It is DMD-based and models the instantaneous velocity
with the auxiliary network v ϕ v_{\phi} , which is refitted to the current rollouts at
every iteration, so the baseline x ~ base = x ~ aux \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}} follows the
policy; since this baseline is fixed within an update, reward augmentation uses
the direction A ⁡ ( v cond − v ϕ ) A\,(v_{\mathrm{cond}}-v_{\phi}) instead of one based on the directional-difference
estimate Equation ( 87 ). This fast increase coincides with the large held-out
degradation; at its first checkpoint with OCR accuracy above 0.82 0.82 , HPSv3
drops from 12.86 12.86 to 5.05 5.05 and ImageReward from 1.233 1.233 to 0.092 0.092 . (iii) In the mixed-reward setting, FewStepOPSD and ReFL achieve the two
highest training rewards, with FewStepOPSD highest at the final iteration.
Using the gradient of the full reward, the two raise the training reward from 1.450 1.450 to 1.64 1.64 and 1.62 1.62 , against 1.46 1.46 – 1.52 1.52 for the five
group-advantage methods, and they also lead on ImageReward and GenEval2. Their
curves nearly coincide ( Figure 4 ); the logged coefficient magnitudes of
FewStepOPSD differ by 0.24 0.24 between the two branches, i.e. 2.4 % 2.4\% of their
fixed sum 1 / β = 10 1/\beta=10 , although the two
reward-augmentation vectors also depend on their different increments
( Section D.3 ). Among the five group-advantage methods, DMDNFT and
MeanFlowNFT come next and perform similarly (training reward 1.51 1.51 – 1.52 1.52 ,
GenEval2 0.41 0.41 at iteration 400 400 ). (iv) In the default mixed-reward configuration, none of the five
group-advantage runs increases CLIPScore, which decreases slightly from 0.289 0.289 to 0.279 0.279 – 0.285 0.285 , whereas FewStepOPSD and ReFL raise it to 0.317 0.317 – 0.322 0.322 . Dedicated CLIP-focused group-advantage ablations do increase
it ( Section D.2 ).

blocks.en:
We measure efficiency by the time per iteration
( Table 7 ) and the time to reach the best checkpoint
( Figure 5 a). It can be observed that (i) The two reward-gradient-based methods are the cheapest per iteration, 219 219 s for ReFL and 268 268 s for FewStepOPSD, because they compute one update
direction per member in the clean-sample space with one query of u θ u_{\theta} instead of four ( n it = 1 n_{\mathrm{it}}=1 ), and because J J cancels in their loss.
However, their sampling time, which includes the reward-coupled rollout of Equation ( 82 ), is 175 175 – 225 225 s per iteration, against about 78 78 s
for the plain rollout of the other five methods ( Table 7 ). Since the
reward is defined in pixel space, its gradient with respect to the clean latent
requires back-propagation through both the reward model and the VAE decoder. (ii) The directional-difference evaluations Equation ( 87 ) and Equation ( 109 ) for the shared- J J v-form plausibly account for most of the cost difference.
FewStepGRPO, MeanFlowAWM and MeanFlowNFT require two additional forward
passes of u old u_{\mathrm{old}} per query. These methods take 423 423 – 435 435 s, against 304 304 – 326 326 s for DMDAWM and DMDNFT, which compute
the baseline from v ϕ v_{\phi} and compute no J J . The difference arises in the
update time ( 344 344 – 355 355 against 223 223 – 245 245 s), and the OCR setting gives
the same ordering ( 451 451 – 496 496 against 342 342 – 346 346 s). (iii) ReFL has a marginally higher best GenEval2 point estimate than
FewStepOPSD ( 0.465 0.465 against 0.463 0.463 ), but the 0.002 0.002 gap is below the stated 0.03 0.03 resolution and does not separate the two methods. ReFL reaches its
selected checkpoint after 12.2 12.2 h (iteration 200 200 ), whereas FewStepOPSD
continues to iteration 400 400 ( 29.8 29.8 h);

initialisation ( 15.89 15.89 against 16.54 16.54 ), and its TA drops markedly, from 1.85 1.85 to 1.23 1.23 . Among the group-advantage-based methods DMDNFT is the most

blocks.en: 6.5 Test-Time Scaling Analysis
blocks.zh: 6.5 (中文(简体) ). 试验时间放大分析

blocks.en:
In deployment, a few-step model should ideally support several operating
points on the quality–latency trade-off, using its training step count for
most requests and more sampling steps when higher quality is required. This
motivates training at a small M step M_{\mathrm{step}} while allowing more solver
steps at inference. If quality improves without retraining, the model supports
test-time scaling and can trade compute for output quality.
Flexible-step generation and inference-time scaling have also been studied for
consistency-type models, improved MeanFlow and scalable generators ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2025a ) ;
our experiment is restricted to the checkpoints and solver grid below.

blocks.en:
Figure 7 shows the per-step trends, and Table S3 in Appendix D reports the percentage changes. We
draw four conclusions. (i) Models at different training stages show different
test-time scaling behaviour. The pretrained SD3.5-Medium models the instantaneous velocity, so four Euler
steps are far too coarse; its scores rise sharply from four to eight steps and
keep improving more slowly up to 32 32 steps (HPSv3 from − 4.49 -4.49 to 9.96 9.96 , Figure 7 ).
Even at 32 32 steps, i.e., 64 64 network evaluations, it remains below every
fine-tuned model at four steps in HPSv3, ImageReward, the aesthetic score,
HPSv2 and PickScore. In contrast, the AnyFlow initialisation, distilled from
SD3.5-Medium for few-step sampling, appears to have already fixed its output patterns at
the step count used in training, and its HPSv3, ImageReward and GenEval2 drop
markedly with more steps; for example, from 4 4 to 32 32 steps, ImageReward
falls from 1.11 1.11 to 1.02 1.02 and GenEval2 from 0.363 0.363 to 0.320 0.320 ( Figure 7 ), beyond the ∼ 0.03 {\sim}0.03 resolution. By comparison, the RL fine-tuned models, which all
start from this initialisation, fluctuate less in these three evaluators. (ii) There is no systematic gain on the training reward. Across the fine-tuned models, the three reward summands remain nearly flat
( Figure 7 and Table S3 ). From 4 4 to 32 32 steps, the held-out
HPSv3 changes by between + 1.0 % +1.0\% and − 6.8 % -6.8\% for six of the seven trainers,
compared with − 17 % -17\% for the AnyFlow initialisation ( Figure 7 ). The stronger degradation
of the initialisation itself suggests that the decline in rewards of the fine-tuned
models is inherited from the initialisation rather than introduced by RL
fine-tuning. Further, these small changes are consistent with the 4 4 -step outputs already having settled into patterns that score well under the
training reward, including sampler-specific reward exploitation.
Doubling to M step = 8 M_{\mathrm{step}}=8 often preserves or slightly improves a
score, but the gain generally saturates or reverses as the grid is refined
further. Figure 8 shows both behaviours; MeanFlowAWM improves at
eight steps and then declines, whereas ReFL declines gradually. (iii) OCR-sensitive prompts can expose a much sharper failure mode. The selected failures occur on malformed or OCR-heavy
prompts. A clear example is shown in Figure 10 , where the DMDNFT and MeanFlowNFT
samples collapse
at M step = 32 M_{\mathrm{step}}=32 to little more than foreground text. HPSv3 falls
from 12.18 12.18 to 0.32 0.32 and from 11.36 11.36 to 0.32 0.32 , respectively, even as
CLIPScore rises from 0.275 0.275 to 0.324 0.324 and from 0.292 0.292 to 0.309 0.309 .
In these selected cases, additional solver steps produce increasingly
text-dominated outputs rather than a visual-quality improvement. (iv) Visible sample-level scaling exists. On inspection, many samples improve with 2 2 – 4 4 times as many
sampling steps, even though the aggregate rewards barely change; on the
selected samples, HPSv3 does rise ( Figure 10 ). At four steps, they
have weak clarity or unstable details, while eight or sixteen steps yield
cleaner and more stable generations; Figure 10 shows two such
cases. The aggregate rewards thus appear less sensitive to these improvements than visual
inspection, and test-time scaling may be useful beyond what the aggregate scores
suggest, although more steps do not improve quality monotonically.

blocks.en: 6.6 Practical Guidance
blocks.zh: 6.6 实用指南

blocks.en:
The empirical results, each from a single run, suggest the following guidance: (i) Where it is affordable, the reward gradient is our recommended
approach. Driving the update directly by ∇ R \nabla R was the most effective choice
in our mixed-reward image experiments; FewStepOPSD and ReFL achieve the two highest
training rewards in the mixed-reward setting and improve all three summands
(§ 6.3 ). However, the applicability of these methods is
restricted in practice. (i) The gradient can become too expensive when the
reward model and the decoder are large or the latent token sequence is long, as
on video (§ 6.4 ). (ii) The reward must be differentiable
with respect to the clean sample, which excludes OCR accuracy
and VideoAlign’s MQ and TA (§ 6.1 , Section D.5 ). Where both conditions hold, ReFL alone is
already a strong baseline in our runs. (ii) Otherwise, group-advantage-based methods apply. When the reward
gradient is too expensive or unavailable, the reward enters only through the
group advantage, and these methods must convert the average velocity into the
instantaneous one (§ 4.3 ). Among them, the DMD-based methods,
which estimate the instantaneous velocity with the auxiliary network v ϕ v_{\phi} ,
have a lower per-iteration cost in the image setting but a higher one on
video, depending on the relative cost of the saved forward passes for J J and
the added forward and backward passes of v ϕ v_{\phi} (§ 6.3 ,
§ 6.4 ). They need extra optimisation
steps and memory for v ϕ v_{\phi} , and in some of the reported runs their larger reward gains coincide
with larger held-out degradation. (iii) Among the group-advantage-based methods, the DiffusionNFT family
reached high reward values in relatively few iterations. The
FlowGRPO-style replay of FewStepGRPO optimises slowly and has the weakest
observed reward endpoints within the common iteration budget: it barely improves
the mixed reward on images and loses the most reward on video. The DiffusionNFT family
reached high reward values within the common iteration budget in both settings, although the cost
per iteration varies; MeanFlowNFT is expensive in the image setting and DMDNFT
on video. AWM mostly lies between the two in the reported reward outcomes and uses a
PPO-style clip to limit each update. (iv) Test-time scaling of the fine-tuned few-step models saturates quickly. Aggregate scores show no systematic gain; three of the seven HPSv3 curves
peak at the training step count of four and one is tied between four and
eight steps ( Table S3 ). By visual inspection, however, many
individual samples look cleaner with 2 2 – 4 4 times as many steps before the
effect saturates or reverses. Additional steps therefore improve the visual
quality of some samples but do not improve aggregate scores monotonically
(§ 6.5 ), and can degrade sample quality on OCR-sensitive prompts.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
Few-step generators reduce the rollout cost that typically dominates RL post-training of
diffusion models, but they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas
existing RL objectives assume an instantaneous velocity and a many-step
sampler. This paper adapts these objectives to few-step models systematically
in three phases and compares the resulting methods within one codebase. The
transformation to x x -space expresses each objective we consider through a
common policy prediction. The decomposition writes the gradient of each
objective as the sum of a reward-free self-regression and a reward
augmentation, so that a method reduces to a choice of three anchors and three
weights. The adaptation computes these anchors from a few-step model, at the
end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity
recovered from the network itself through the MeanFlow identity (the
self-induced velocity) or from an auxiliary network. The seven resulting trainers share one training step and are
compared under shared rollout, reward and evaluation code, each in a single
run. Where the reward
is differentiable and its gradient affordable, FewStepOPSD and ReFL, which use
the reward gradient, were the most effective. Otherwise, the DiffusionNFT family
reached high rewards in relatively few iterations, and the DMD-based
variants were faster per iteration on image but slower on video, depending on
the relative cost of forward and backward passes, and in some runs coincided
with larger held-out degradation.
For the fine-tuned models, additional sampling steps gave no systematic
aggregate gain, although many individual samples improve with two to four
times as many steps as in training.

blocks.en:
Several questions remain open. (i) The DMD-based variants estimate the instantaneous velocity with an
auxiliary network, which requires
additional forward and backward passes to fit this network and GPU memory to
hold it. How to reduce this overhead remains open. (ii) Reward-gradient-based methods require a reward that is differentiable
with respect to the clean sample and a gradient that fits in memory. On video,
the motion-quality and text-alignment terms of VideoAlign provide no gradient,
and the per-frame decoding required by GPU memory makes the gradient deviate
strongly from that of a joint decode. Cheaper and more faithful reward
gradients for long latent sequences are needed. (iii) With a scalar group advantage in the mixed-reward setting, whether every reward summand takes effect
depends on the weighting of the summands, on the rescaling by the
global-batch standard deviation in Equation ( 83 ), and on the small
within-group spread of some summands ( Section D.2 ). A general and more
reliable construction of the group advantage remains open. (iv) In our experiments, a few-step model fine-tuned at one step count does not improve
systematically with more steps. Fine-tuning at more step counts may give
test-time scaling but makes the rollouts more expensive. Whether it can be
introduced cheaply during training, or without training, so that a model
fine-tuned at a small step count still improves with more steps at test time,
remains open.

reported variant.
